faq.a: Yes, if they have severe hypoxia or hypercapnia; look for retractions and altered mental status.
faq.q: Can a patient be in respiratory distress with a normal respiratory rate?

exam: What bedside signs would you look for to decide if a patient needs immediate oxygen? — Count retractions, cyanosis, SpO₂ < 90 %, inability to speak.

A 7‑year‑old with sickle‑cell disease presents with tachypnoea, subcostal retractions and a SpO₂ of 88 %. What is your next step? — Start O₂, assess for acute chest syndrome, obtain chest X‑ray and give empiric antibiotics.
How does tripod positioning improve ventilation? — It stabilises the shoulder girdle, allowing accessory muscles to lift the rib cage more effectively.

Differentiate between respiratory distress caused by severe malaria versus bacterial pneumonia on exam. — Malaria often has high fever, splenomegaly, and no focal chest signs; pneumonia shows crackles, localized retractions, and possible pleural effusion.
Why is pulse oximetry preferred over clinical cyanosis in dark‑skinned patients? — Cyanosis may be invisible; SpO₂ provides an objective measure.
When is it appropriate to withhold bronchodilators in a distressed patient? — In pure hypoxic respiratory failure without bronchospasm, as they may cause tachycardia without benefit.
Explain the physiological reason for intercostal retractions in distress. — Negative intrathoracic pressure pulls the soft tissue inward when inspiratory effort exceeds chest wall compliance.
What are the red‑flag laboratory results that mandate ICU transfer? — PaCO₂ > 60 mmHg, pH < 7.20, lactate > 4 mmol/L, or rapidly falling SpO₂ despite maximal O₂.
ai.title: Signs of Respiratory Distress
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Recognise and interpret the bedside signs that indicate respiratory distress, understand their pathophysiology, common tropical causes, and urgent actions needed in low‑resource settings.

b: Often presents with tachypnoea, use of accessory muscles, and altered mental status.
In low‑resource hospitals, diagnosis relies heavily on physical signs.
sections.p: Respiratory distress is a clinical syndrome where the patient cannot maintain adequate ventilation without increased work of breathing. It signals impending respiratory failure and requires rapid assessment.

b: Mild: tachypnoea, nasal flaring, mild intercostal retractions.
Moderate: marked retractions, tripod position, paradoxical breathing.
Severe: altered consciousness, inability to speak, cyanosis.
sections.p: The severity of distress is graded by the number and intensity of signs, the PaO₂/PaCO₂ trends (when available), and the patient’s ability to speak.

b: Early identification guides oxygen therapy, bronchodilators, antibiotics, or antimalarials.
Missing severe signs leads to rapid decompensation and death.
sections.p: In East African hospitals the most common precipitants are pneumonia (including TB), asthma, COPD from biomass exposure, severe malaria, sickle‑cell crisis, and cardiac failure from rheumatic heart disease.

b: 1. Tachypnoea (>30 breaths/min in adults).
2. Nasal flaring (increased airflow resistance).
3. Intercostal retractions.
4. Subcostal retractions.
5. Suprasternal retractions.
6. Use of accessory muscles (sternocleidomastoid, scalene).
7. Tripod positioning.
8. Paradoxical abdominal movement.
9. Cyanosis (lips, nail beds).
10. Altered mental status (agitation or lethargy).
11. Inability to complete a full sentence.
sections.p: Examiners expect you to list the 11 classic bedside signs, explain their physiological basis, and prioritise management steps.
In low‑resource settings, investigations are guided by what will change management.

t.b: Is the patient hypoxic? – SpO₂ < 90 % indicates need for supplemental O₂.
Is there hypercapnia or severe acidosis? – PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg or pH < 7.30 signals impending failure.
What is the radiographic pattern? – Consolidation suggests pneumonia; cardiomegaly suggests heart failure.
Is malaria contributing? – Positive test directs antimalarial therapy.
Is TB present? – Positive smear guides anti‑TB treatment.

b: Give supplemental O₂ to keep SpO₂ ≥ 94 % (or ≥ 90 % in COPD).
Bronchodilators (e.g., salbutamol) for asthma or COPD exacerbations.
Antibiotics for bacterial pneumonia; consider TB regimen if smear positive.
IV artesunate for severe malaria.
Treat anaemia or sickle‑cell crisis with transfusion if indicated.
Position patient upright or in tripod; avoid supine if severe retractions.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then support ventilation and monitor for deterioration.

b: Sepsis with metabolic acidosis – may cause tachypnoea without true airway obstruction.
Anxiety/panic attack – rapid breathing but normal oxygenation and no retractions.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic respiratory distress but have different primary pathology.

b: Peripheral cyanosis may be absent in dark‑skinned patients; rely on SpO₂.
Normal chest X‑ray early in pulmonary edema; clinical signs take precedence.
sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or misleading findings.
